name: Codon Plot Calculator
seoDesc: A codon plot shows where the rare codons sit along a coding sequence, not just how many there are. Free codon plot calculator: enter your values and get codon
summary:
A codon plot shows where the rare codons sit along a coding sequence, not just how many there are. It returns codons read, rare codons (w ≤ 0.2) and runs of 3+ rare codons, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It scores every codon for E. coli adaptation, draws the sequence as a track of bars and lists runs of rare codons — the clusters that stall a ribosome and cost protein yield. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Codon Plot
sections.html:
plot the relative adaptiveness w of each codon in order; a cluster is 3 or more consecutive codons with w ≤ 0.2

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
wrelative adaptiveness of the codon in E. coli0 – 1
windowcodons per summary point on the plotcodons
clusterconsecutive rare codonscodons

sections.title: How do I use the Codon Plot?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Paste the coding sequence — the page reads from the first base as codon 1.
  2. Set the window if you want the summary coarser or finer than 30 codons.
  3. Read the track first: a flat blue line with a handful of dips is a healthy gene. Then read the cluster list — a run of three or more rare codons is the part worth resynthesising.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: window size of 30 codons.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
no clusterEventhe gene has rare codons but they are spread out — usually fine
one clusterOne hot spotoften at the 5′ end; check the translation initiation region
two or threeSeveral hot spotsexpect a yield penalty; consider changing those codons
four or morePoorly adaptedresynthesise the gene rather than tune single codons

  • This is the plot that shows what a single CAI number cannot: a gene with a good average can still carry five consecutive codons at w = 0.06, and that run is what the ribosome queues on.

  • The y-axis is relative adaptiveness, not frequency. w = 1.00 means the codon is the host's most-used synonym for that amino acid; w = 0.03 means it is nearly unused.

  • Positions are codon numbers, not base numbers, so position 12 is bases 34–36.

  • Met, Trp and stop codons carry no adaptiveness — they are drawn as neutral points rather than scored, because there is no choice to make.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Plotting a genomic sequence with introns: the frame breaks at the first intron and every codon after it is wrong.
  • Treating a low average as the whole story, or a high one as a clean bill of health.
  • Ignoring an all-rare cluster at the very start, which affects initiation more than internal clusters affect elongation.

faq.q: What does a codon plot show that the CAI does not?
faq.a: Position. CAI averages the whole sequence; the plot shows where the rare codons are, so a cluster that stalls translation is visible instead of averaged away.

faq.q: What counts as a rare codon?
faq.a: Here, a codon whose relative adaptiveness in E. coli is 0.2 or below — roughly the bottom fifth of the usage range. The cut-off is stated on the page rather than implied.

faq.q: Why are the stops and Met not scored?
faq.a: Because they have a single codon. Adaptiveness measures a choice between synonyms, and there is none for those.

faq.q: Can I use the plot for a human gene?
faq.a: The weighting table here is E. coli. For a mammalian expression experiment the pattern of rare codons differs, and the codon adaptation index page lets you switch the host.

faq.q: What does the Codon Plot actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns codons read, rare codons (w ≤ 0.2) and runs of 3+ rare codons. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.
